Lessons.Title: What are Scaled Copies?
ExplanationParagraphs: Edulytiks learning target: Recognize scaled copies by testing whether every corresponding length changes by the same factor; explain why a distorted figure is not scaled. This is independently authored Grade 7 mathematics teaching aligned to the 2017–2019 OUR/IM source lesson. Source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/2/1/1/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0 source lineage; no publisher artwork reproduced).

A picture can look similar without being a mathematically valid scaled copy. Check the length of each corresponding segment, not only a single edge. The calculations and figures in the following examples were created for Edulytiks; they do not claim to reproduce the publisher's tasks or Cool Down.

Student task alignment: This lesson requires learners to sort scaled and distorted figures, create a scaled letter or polygon and explain their partner's classification. Learner-produced figures, justification and peer discussion require teacher review; a numeric Practice score alone cannot certify that source goal.

First-party F-classification activity (independent Edulytiks reconstruction, not publisher artwork): Use the additional candidate-dimensions table below to classify seven possible copies of an upright block F. The original F has an upright 4-unit spine, 2-unit top bar and 1-unit short bar. For each candidate, check all three matching length ratios AND whether every corresponding corner angle remains equal. Draw a valid copy with a new factor on squared paper, label its parts, and explain your decision to a partner; a teacher must inspect the finished outline and explanation. Table values specify candidate measurements rather than the publisher's visual figures.

KeyConcepts.Title: Corresponding lengths
KeyConcepts.Definition: A pair of matching lengths in the original and its copy.
KeyConcepts.Rule: All corresponding-length ratios must equal one positive factor.
KeyConcepts.Example: Side lengths 3, 4, 5 and 6, 8, 10 all have factor 2.

KeyConcepts.Title: Same multiplier
KeyConcepts.Definition: Every length is multiplied by one common factor k greater than zero.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check more than one segment; k must be constant.
KeyConcepts.Example: 3→6 and 4→8 both use k=2.

KeyConcepts.Title: Not scaled
KeyConcepts.Definition: A drawing stretched by different horizontal and vertical factors is distorted.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Unequal corresponding ratios disprove a scaled copy.
KeyConcepts.Example: A 3-by-4 rectangle changed to 6-by-7 has factors 2 and 7/4.

WorkedExamples.Title: Prove a scaled triangle
WorkedExamples.Question: A triangle has side lengths 3, 4 and 5 units. Another has corresponding lengths 6, 8 and 10. Is the second a scaled copy?
WorkedExamples.Method: Compare ratios for all three matched sides.
Steps: Compute 10÷5=2 and confirm the same positive factor.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Yes, every corresponding side is doubled, so the scale factor is 2.
WorkedExamples.Check: The side lengths preserve one common multiplier.

WorkedExamples.Title: Reject a stretched shape
WorkedExamples.Question: A rectangle measures 3 by 4 cm. A proposed copy measures 6 by 7 cm. Is it scaled?
Steps: The two factors differ, so no uniform scale exists.
WorkedExamples.Check: No choice of one k makes both sides match.

WorkedExamples.Title: Make a scaled rectangle
WorkedExamples.Question: A rectangle measures 2 by 5 units. Make a scaled copy with factor 1.5.
WorkedExamples.Check: Both corresponding dimensions use factor 1.5.

WorkedExamples.Title: Sort, draw, and defend scaled F-shape models
WorkedExamples.Question: Draw an original block letter F from vertices in order (0,0),(4,0),(4,1),(1,1),(1,2),(3,2),(3,3),(1,3),(1,5),(0,5). On graph paper make a scale-factor-2 copy and a horizontal-only stretch x→2x; which drawing is a scaled copy, and why?
WorkedExamples.Method: Plot and connect every vertex in order; compare both horizontal and vertical corresponding segments and orally justify the distinction to a partner.
Steps: Draw and close the original ten-vertex F outline; distinguish segment positions by the vertex labels.
For a factor-2 copy multiply both x and y of each vertex by 2, then connect in the same order.
For the horizontal-only stretch double x but keep y unchanged; a 4-unit top becomes 8 while a 5-unit spine stays 5.
Use multiple corresponding horizontal and vertical segments and show the figures to a teacher for a drawing/justification rubric.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Only doubling both coordinates gives a scaled copy with scale factor 2; horizontal-only stretching does not.
WorkedExamples.Check: A teacher verifies the actual F outlines and student explanation, not just the two ratios.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Adding the same length to every side
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Adding 2 to sides 3 and 4 produces multipliers 5/3 and 6/4, not one factor.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Multiply each length by k; never replace uniform scaling with constant addition.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Checking only one side
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: One ratio can match by accident while other dimensions are distorted.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Calculate the factor for every available corresponding length.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating a correctly computed numerical value as proof the complete drawing, construction, explanation or measured source task is satisfactory.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original activity includes creating or interpreting mathematical representations and defending the work to another person.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check every corresponding quantity, an accurate student sketch/measurement and written or oral justification with a teacher rubric; treat auto-marked arithmetic only as supporting practice.

SummaryPoints: Every corresponding length changes by one positive multiplier.
A visually plausible drawing can still be distorted.
Explain a scaled-copy decision with at least two checked corresponding ratios.

Lessons.Title: Corresponding Parts and Scale Factors
ExplanationParagraphs: Edulytiks learning target: Identify matching points, segments and angles in two figures, then calculate and explain the scale factor. This is independently authored Grade 7 mathematics teaching aligned to the 2017–2019 OUR/IM source lesson. Source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/2/1/2/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0 source lineage; no publisher artwork reproduced).

The word corresponding identifies parts that play the same role in each figure. Scale factors compare corresponding lengths; corresponding angle measures remain equal. The calculations and figures in the following examples were created for Edulytiks; they do not claim to reproduce the publisher's tasks or Cool Down.

Student task alignment: This lesson requires learners to identify corresponding points, sides and angles, and check scales with physical tracing or drawing. Learner-produced figures, justification and peer discussion require teacher review; a numeric Practice score alone cannot certify that source goal.

KeyConcepts.Title: Corresponding vertices
KeyConcepts.Definition: Points in the original and copy with matching positions.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Follow vertex order consistently.
KeyConcepts.Example: In triangles ABC and DEF, A↔D, B↔E, C↔F.

KeyConcepts.Title: Scale factor
KeyConcepts.Definition: A common ratio of a copied length to its matching original length.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Find k=copy length/original length.
KeyConcepts.Example: Side AB=4 and DE=6 give k=6/4=1.5.

KeyConcepts.Title: Angle preservation
KeyConcepts.Definition: Uniform scaling changes lengths but not the measure of an angle.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Compare matched vertices, not arbitrary nearby angles.
KeyConcepts.Example: If angle B is 60°, its counterpart E is 60°.

WorkedExamples.Title: Match all sides
WorkedExamples.Question: ABC has AB=4, BC=5, CA=6; DEF has DE=6, EF=7.5, FD=9. Find the scale factor.
Steps: Match AB to DE, BC to EF and CA to FD.
WorkedExamples.Check: All three paired lengths use 1.5.

WorkedExamples.Title: Reverse the scale
WorkedExamples.Question: Triangle DEF is a 1.5-scale copy of ABC. What factor returns DEF to ABC?
WorkedExamples.Check: The original corresponding length 4 is restored.

WorkedExamples.Title: Corresponding angles
WorkedExamples.Question: ABC has angle measures 40°, 60°, 80° and DEF is its uniformly scaled copy with A↔D, B↔E, C↔F. Find angle E.
Steps: Identify that B corresponds to E.
Scaling preserves angles, so angle E=60°.
WorkedExamples.Check: The total remains 180° for both triangles.

WorkedExamples.Title: Label corresponding vertices, sides, and angles in two copies
WorkedExamples.Question: Draw triangle ABC with A=(0,0), B=(4,0), C=(0,3). Draw DEF with D=(0,0), E=(6,0), F=(0,4.5). Identify the counterparts of point B, segment BC, and angle BAC. Explain a scale factor and measure or compare the right angle.
WorkedExamples.Method: Draw both polygons, maintain matching vertex order, and compare segment ratios and the included right angle.
Steps: Plot the three original and three copy vertices on coordinate grid with half-unit marks.
Follow vertex order A↔D, B↔E, C↔F: B corresponds to E; BC to EF; angle BAC to angle EDF.
Corresponding leg ratios are 6/4=1.5 and 4.5/3=1.5; the hypotenuses are 5 and 7.5.
Confirm angle BAC and EDF are right angles; submit the labeled drawing and oral explanation for teacher review.
WorkedExamples.Answer: B↔E, BC↔EF, ∠BAC↔∠EDF; k=3/2 and both angles are 90°.
WorkedExamples.Check: A correct calculation without correctly labeled corresponding points/angles does not complete the activity.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Pairing nonmatching sides
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A ratio of unrelated sides is not a scale factor.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Label corresponding vertices first, then compare matching segments.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Multiplying angle measures by the scale factor
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Scale changes lengths, not angle sizes.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Keep corresponding angles equal in a scaled copy.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating a correctly computed numerical value as proof the complete drawing, construction, explanation or measured source task is satisfactory.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original activity includes creating or interpreting mathematical representations and defending the work to another person.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check every corresponding quantity, an accurate student sketch/measurement and written or oral justification with a teacher rubric; treat auto-marked arithmetic only as supporting practice.

SummaryPoints: Corresponding points and sides are matched by their roles.
The copy-to-original length ratio is the scale factor.
Reciprocal factors reverse scaling; angles remain unchanged.

Lessons.Title: Making Scaled Copies
ExplanationParagraphs: Edulytiks learning target: Draw figures with a specified factor and justify that every side and distance is multiplied, not increased additively. This is independently authored Grade 7 mathematics teaching aligned to the 2017–2019 OUR/IM source lesson. Source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/2/1/3/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0 source lineage; no publisher artwork reproduced).

On a coordinate grid, a scale centered at the origin multiplies both coordinates by the same factor. A scaled drawing must preserve its shape and corresponding angle measures. The calculations and figures in the following examples were created for Edulytiks; they do not claim to reproduce the publisher's tasks or Cool Down.

Student task alignment: This lesson requires learners to construct scaled copies both on and off the grid, and critique additive as opposed to multiplicative methods. Learner-produced figures, justification and peer discussion require teacher review; a numeric Practice score alone cannot certify that source goal.

KeyConcepts.Title: Coordinate scaling
KeyConcepts.Definition: A point (x,y) becomes (kx,ky) for a scale centered at (0,0).
KeyConcepts.Rule: Apply the same positive k to both coordinates.
KeyConcepts.Example: (2,3) becomes (4,6) when k=2.

KeyConcepts.Title: Multiplicative sides
KeyConcepts.Definition: Corresponding lengths are related by products.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use new length=k×original length.
KeyConcepts.Example: Length 3 becomes 6 under k=2.

KeyConcepts.Title: Construction check
KeyConcepts.Definition: Scaled drawings preserve angle measures and length ratios.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check horizontal, vertical and sloping matching distances.
KeyConcepts.Example: A right triangle with legs 2 and 3 scales to legs 4 and 6 at k=2.

WorkedExamples.Title: Scale on a grid
WorkedExamples.Question: A triangle has vertices (0,0), (2,0) and (0,3). Draw a factor-2 copy.
WorkedExamples.Method: Scale each coordinate from the origin.
Steps: Multiply (0,3) by 2 to get (0,6), then join the vertices.
WorkedExamples.Check: Both legs and the hypotenuse are doubled.

WorkedExamples.Title: Reject addition as a scaling operation
WorkedExamples.Question: Original legs measure 2 and 3 units. A pupil adds 2 to each, producing legs 4 and 5. Is this a factor-2 copy?
Steps: One common multiplier does not exist.
WorkedExamples.Check: A factor-2 copy would have legs 4 and 6.

WorkedExamples.Title: Draw a half-size copy
WorkedExamples.Question: Triangle vertices are (0,0), (6,0), (0,4). Use factor 1/2.
WorkedExamples.Method: Multiply both nonzero coordinates by one half.
Steps: Send (0,4) to (0,2) and join the points.
WorkedExamples.Check: The legs change 6→3 and 4→2 consistently.

WorkedExamples.Title: Construct two scaled L-shaped polygons and critique additive resizing
WorkedExamples.Question: Make an L-polygon by joining (0,0),(6,0),(6,2),(4,2),(4,5),(0,5). Draw copies at scale factors 1/2 and 3. A student proposes adding 2 to every side length instead. What goes wrong?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use a coordinate grid to construct both scaled figures, explain the multiplier for every corresponding segment, and compare to an additive claim.
Steps: Draw the original outline and check it closes without crossed edges.
For factor 1/2, plot vertices (0,0),(3,0),(3,1),(2,1),(2,2.5),(0,2.5) and join in the same order.
For factor 3, plot (0,0),(18,0),(18,6),(12,6),(12,15),(0,15) and join in the same order.
Two original sides of lengths 6 and 2 become 8 and 4 by adding 2, giving unequal ratios 8/6 and 4/2: reject the additive strategy.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Both independently drawn copies preserve the L shape under factors 1/2 and 3. Adding 2 per side does not give one uniform factor.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher checks both actual outlines, vertex order, non-overlap and a written comparison of additive vs multiplicative strategies.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Moving every point by the same offset
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Translation moves the figure without changing its size.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Multiply distances from the chosen center to construct a scaled copy.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Scaling only the horizontal coordinate
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Unequal changes on x and y distort angles and side ratios.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use the same multiplier on x and y when scaling from the origin.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating a correctly computed numerical value as proof the complete drawing, construction, explanation or measured source task is satisfactory.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original activity includes creating or interpreting mathematical representations and defending the work to another person.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check every corresponding quantity, an accurate student sketch/measurement and written or oral justification with a teacher rubric; treat auto-marked arithmetic only as supporting practice.

SummaryPoints: Draw scaled copies by multiplying corresponding lengths by k.
Use (kx,ky) to scale grid coordinates about the origin.
Verify both shape preservation and matching length ratios.

Visuals.Description: Each coordinate is multiplied by 2; the origin stays fixed. This first-party text table has labeled row headers so its numerical evidence is accessible without color or an image.

Lessons.Title: Scaled Relationships
ExplanationParagraphs: Edulytiks learning target: Test corresponding distances even between unjoined points and verify that matched angle measures stay equal. This is independently authored Grade 7 mathematics teaching aligned to the 2017–2019 OUR/IM source lesson. Source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/2/1/4/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0 source lineage; no publisher artwork reproduced).

In a true scaled copy, the relationship applies to every distance, including an invisible diagonal between two vertices; corresponding angles remain equal. The calculations and figures in the following examples were created for Edulytiks; they do not claim to reproduce the publisher's tasks or Cool Down.

Student task alignment: This lesson requires learners to measure corresponding angles and unconnected vertex distances with a ruler/protractor. Learner-produced figures, justification and peer discussion require teacher review; a numeric Practice score alone cannot certify that source goal.

KeyConcepts.Title: Unmarked distances
KeyConcepts.Definition: A distance between two points is still scaled even when no segment is drawn.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check vertex-to-vertex distances as well as displayed sides.
KeyConcepts.Example: A diagonal of length 5 becomes 10 at k=2.

KeyConcepts.Title: Right-triangle distance
KeyConcepts.Definition: Perpendicular offsets can locate a diagonal by the Pythagorean theorem.
KeyConcepts.Rule: For legs a and b, diagonal=√(a²+b²).
KeyConcepts.Example: Offsets 3 and 4 give distance 5.

KeyConcepts.Title: Corresponding angles
KeyConcepts.Definition: Uniform scaling preserves all angle measures.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use matching vertices or a protractor to compare angles.
KeyConcepts.Example: A 90° corner remains 90° after doubling all lengths.

WorkedExamples.Title: Test a hidden diagonal
WorkedExamples.Question: Two vertices are 3 across and 4 up. In a proposed factor-2 copy they are 6 across and 8 up. Find both distances.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use right triangles for the two point separations.
WorkedExamples.Check: Both horizontal and vertical changes use factor 2.

WorkedExamples.Title: Check an angle
WorkedExamples.Question: A quadrilateral corner measures 70°. A scaled copy is created with k=3. What is the corresponding angle?
Steps: Scaling changes lengths, not directions of each corresponding side.
WorkedExamples.Check: Multiplying 70 by 3 would be incorrect.

WorkedExamples.Title: Detect nonuniform distortion
WorkedExamples.Question: A 3-by-4 right-angled shape is copied as a 6-by-6 shape. Is it scaled?
Steps: Unequal ratios disprove a scaled copy.
WorkedExamples.Check: The original diagonal is 5; copy diagonal √72, not 10.

WorkedExamples.Title: Test an unconnected distance with a ruler
WorkedExamples.Question: On a 1-unit grid, plot A=(0,0), B=(4,0), C=(0,3) and scaled counterparts D=(0,0), E=(8,0), F=(0,6). The lines BC and EF are not drawn. Without relying on a formula from a later grade, measure or estimate both distances with a ruler. What should hold?
WorkedExamples.Method: Draw the two polygons and use a ruler/protractor to compare corresponding but previously unconnected vertices and angles.
Steps: Mark the point pairs and identify the scale factor 2 from the horizontal and vertical offsets.
Use a ruler or tracing overlay to measure unjoined BC and EF (approximately 5 and 10 units respectively).
Check that the two measured distances are in an approximate ratio of 2, within measurement precision.
Measure angle BAC and EDF and explain why corresponding angles stay equal.
WorkedExamples.Answer: BC≈5 and EF≈10 grid units; the hidden corresponding distance scales by about 2, while the corresponding angle is unchanged.
WorkedExamples.Check: Accept measured estimates with a justified tolerance; teacher checks the actual sketch and protractor work.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Checking only drawn edges
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Undrawn distances may expose distortions.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Compare multiple distances between matched points, not just labeled segments.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming a larger shape has larger angles
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Uniform enlargement does not increase angle measures.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Compare angle measures separately from length ratios.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating a correctly computed numerical value as proof the complete drawing, construction, explanation or measured source task is satisfactory.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original activity includes creating or interpreting mathematical representations and defending the work to another person.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check every corresponding quantity, an accurate student sketch/measurement and written or oral justification with a teacher rubric; treat auto-marked arithmetic only as supporting practice.

SummaryPoints: Every matched distance scales, drawn or not.
Angles stay equal in scaled copies.
Use distances and angles together to test a proposed copy.

Visuals.Title: Distances in scaled copies
Visuals.Description: Invisible diagonals scale too; horizontal and vertical offsets are doubled. This first-party text table has labeled row headers so its numerical evidence is accessible without color or an image.

Lessons.Title: The Size of the Scale Factor
ExplanationParagraphs: Edulytiks learning target: Explain enlargement, unchanged size and reduction; identify reciprocal factors for reversing a scale. This is independently authored Grade 7 mathematics teaching aligned to the 2017–2019 OUR/IM source lesson. Source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/2/1/5/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0 source lineage; no publisher artwork reproduced).

A positive factor below 1 reduces lengths; factor 1 preserves lengths; a factor above 1 enlarges. The reverse factor is 1/k. The calculations and figures in the following examples were created for Edulytiks; they do not claim to reproduce the publisher's tasks or Cool Down.

Student task alignment: This lesson requires learners to compare factors below, equal to and above one, reconstruct puzzle pieces and revise mismatched copies. Learner-produced figures, justification and peer discussion require teacher review; a numeric Practice score alone cannot certify that source goal.

KeyConcepts.Title: Scale below one
KeyConcepts.Definition: If 0<k<1, every copied length is smaller.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Multiply, do not subtract a fixed amount.
KeyConcepts.Example: 8 cm scaled by 1/2 becomes 4 cm.

KeyConcepts.Title: Scale above one
KeyConcepts.Definition: If k>1, every copied length is larger.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check proportional multiplication.
KeyConcepts.Example: 8 cm scaled by 5/4 becomes 10 cm.

KeyConcepts.Title: Inverse scale
KeyConcepts.Definition: Scaling back requires the reciprocal 1/k.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Multiply the forward and backward factors to get 1.
KeyConcepts.Example: The reverse of 5/4 is 4/5.

WorkedExamples.Title: Classify factors
WorkedExamples.Question: What happens to a 12 cm segment with factors 1/2, 1 and 3/2?
WorkedExamples.Check: All changes follow the factor categories.

WorkedExamples.Title: Reverse a scale
WorkedExamples.Question: A 4 cm side becomes 5 cm. What factor returns it to 4 cm?
WorkedExamples.Check: Forward times reverse equals 1.

WorkedExamples.Title: Return a reduced drawing to full size
WorkedExamples.Question: A shape is reduced by 1/3 and a copied edge is 7 cm. Find the original edge.
WorkedExamples.Check: The copied length is one third of 21.

WorkedExamples.Title: Construct and exchange scaled puzzle tiles
WorkedExamples.Question: A small polygon piece has vertices (0,0),(4,0),(4,2),(0,2). Produce a 1/2-scale copy. A partner receives your copy but not the original; how can they recreate the original piece?
WorkedExamples.Method: Draw the half-size figure on a grid, check all corresponding lengths, then apply the reciprocal scale factor.
Steps: For factor 1/2, make a 2-by-1 rectangle with vertices (0,0),(2,0),(2,1),(0,1).
To restore the missing piece, apply the reciprocal factor 2 to every copy length.
Exchange drawings with another learner and revise any distorted or misaligned edge.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Half-sized piece 2 by 1; to recreate the original piece scale all lengths by 2.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher reviews the actual matched pieces, reciprocal explanation, and any revision.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Calling every k less than 1 a negative scale
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A positive factor below one is a reduction, not a reflection.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Compare k with 0 and 1 separately.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using the same factor in both directions
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Forward and reverse factors must multiply to 1.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use 1/k to recover original lengths.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating a correctly computed numerical value as proof the complete drawing, construction, explanation or measured source task is satisfactory.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original activity includes creating or interpreting mathematical representations and defending the work to another person.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check every corresponding quantity, an accurate student sketch/measurement and written or oral justification with a teacher rubric; treat auto-marked arithmetic only as supporting practice.

SummaryPoints: 0<k<1 reduces, k=1 preserves, k>1 enlarges.
Reverse a scale by using 1/k.
Scaled-copy lengths depend multiplicatively on k.

Visuals.Title: Scale-factor sizes
Visuals.Description: The same 12-unit segment is reduced, preserved, or enlarged depending on k. This first-party text table has labeled row headers so its numerical evidence is accessible without color or an image.

Lessons.Title: Scaling and Area
ExplanationParagraphs: Edulytiks learning target: Find how a two-dimensional shape's area changes under scaling and explain why the multiplier is k squared. This is independently authored Grade 7 mathematics teaching aligned to the 2017–2019 OUR/IM source lesson. Source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/2/1/6/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0 source lineage; no publisher artwork reproduced).

Scaling both dimensions by k multiplies area by k², not k. This optional source lesson uses tangible shapes before numerical area calculations. The calculations and figures in the following examples were created for Edulytiks; they do not claim to reproduce the publisher's tasks or Cool Down.

Student task alignment: This lesson requires learners to build area models from equal tiles and justify a squared area factor. Learner-produced figures, justification and peer discussion require teacher review; a numeric Practice score alone cannot certify that source goal.

KeyConcepts.Title: Area factor
KeyConcepts.Definition: The area of a scaled 2D shape is k² times its original area.
KeyConcepts.Rule: A_new=k²×A_original.
KeyConcepts.Example: At k=2, area quadruples.

KeyConcepts.Title: Rectangle model
KeyConcepts.Definition: Area=length×width, so scaling both makes (kl)(kw)=k²lw.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Multiply each side first and compare areas.
KeyConcepts.Example: 3×4 has area 12; 6×8 has area 48.

KeyConcepts.Title: Reduction of area
KeyConcepts.Definition: A length factor below one squares to an even smaller area factor.
KeyConcepts.Rule: For k=1/2, area becomes 1/4.
KeyConcepts.Example: 80 square units becomes 20.

WorkedExamples.Title: Rectangle enlargement
WorkedExamples.Question: A 3 by 4 rectangle is scaled by 2. Compare its areas.

WorkedExamples.Title: Triangle enlargement
WorkedExamples.Question: A triangle has base 6 and height 4. Scale by 3. Find its new area.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use triangle area before and after scaling.

WorkedExamples.Title: Half-size reduction
WorkedExamples.Question: A polygon has area 80 square units. What is its area when every length is halved?
WorkedExamples.Check: A direct 80÷2=40 would ignore the second dimension.

WorkedExamples.Title: Build a scaled tiling and justify why area grows as the factor squared
WorkedExamples.Question: Build a rectangular mosaic of 3 congruent unit squares in a 3-by-1 strip. How many same-size unit squares are needed for whole-strip scaled copies with side factors 2 and 3? Draw the tiled arrays.
WorkedExamples.Method: Draw and count the squares in each 2D scaled strip rather than multiplying the original square count by k.
Steps: Draw the original 3-by-1 strip and count 3 unit squares.
A side factor of 2 creates a 6-by-2 array, containing 12 unit squares (3×2²).
A side factor of 3 creates a 9-by-3 array, containing 27 unit squares (3×3²).
Use tile rows and columns to explain why doubled lengths imply four times the area, not two times.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 12 unit squares at factor 2 and 27 at factor 3.
WorkedExamples.Check: The student's tile drawings must match the counts and preserve the scaled 3:1 proportions.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Multiplying area by k
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Area depends on two independent dimensions.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Multiply area by k².

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Squaring an area expressed with linear units
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Area is measured in square units.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Keep the units squared after calculating.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating a correctly computed numerical value as proof the complete drawing, construction, explanation or measured source task is satisfactory.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original activity includes creating or interpreting mathematical representations and defending the work to another person.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check every corresponding quantity, an accurate student sketch/measurement and written or oral justification with a teacher rubric; treat auto-marked arithmetic only as supporting practice.

SummaryPoints: Length scale factor k gives area factor k².
Use areas of rectangles, triangles or manipulatives to verify.
The square-factor rule holds for reductions too.

Visuals.Title: Area is squared scaling
Visuals.Description: A 3-by-4 rectangle becomes 6-by-8 at scale factor 2, increasing area fourfold. This first-party text table has labeled row headers so its numerical evidence is accessible without color or an image.

Lessons.Title: Scale Drawings
ExplanationParagraphs: Edulytiks learning target: Interpret scale drawings of real objects and calculate actual and drawing distances with consistent units. This is independently authored Grade 7 mathematics teaching aligned to the 2017–2019 OUR/IM source lesson. Source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/2/1/7/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0 source lineage; no publisher artwork reproduced).

A scale drawing represents distances in the real world on a two-dimensional drawing. A labeled scale relates drawing units to actual distance units. The calculations and figures in the following examples were created for Edulytiks; they do not claim to reproduce the publisher's tasks or Cool Down.

Student task alignment: This lesson requires learners to interpret measurements from an actual drawn scale diagram and draw physical-length segments to scale. Learner-produced figures, justification and peer discussion require teacher review; a numeric Practice score alone cannot certify that source goal.

KeyConcepts.Title: Drawing-to-actual scale
KeyConcepts.Definition: A stated drawing length represents a fixed real-world length.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use equivalent ratios for all distances.
KeyConcepts.Example: 1 cm to 2 m means 3 cm represents 6 m.

KeyConcepts.Title: Actual distance
KeyConcepts.Definition: Multiply drawing distance by the actual amount represented per drawing unit.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Actual=scale value×drawing length.
KeyConcepts.Example: 7 cm on a 1 cm:2 m drawing is 14 m.

KeyConcepts.Title: Drawing distance
KeyConcepts.Definition: Divide actual distance by actual distance per drawing unit.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Drawing=actual distance/scale value.
KeyConcepts.Example: 9 m becomes 4.5 cm when 1 cm represents 2 m.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find an actual wall length
WorkedExamples.Question: A floor plan uses 1 cm to represent 2 m. A wall measures 7 cm on the plan.
WorkedExamples.Check: 14 m÷7 cm gives 2 m per cm.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find a plan length
WorkedExamples.Question: An actual wall is 9 m long; the plan uses 1 cm for 2 m. What should you draw?
WorkedExamples.Method: Divide actual length by 2 m per cm.
WorkedExamples.Check: The scale converts the plan length back to 9 m.

WorkedExamples.Title: Unitless ratio scale
WorkedExamples.Question: A map scale is 1:100 with matching units. A line on the map measures 4 cm.
WorkedExamples.Check: 4 m equals 400 cm.

WorkedExamples.Title: Measure a first-party school-court sketch to infer its real dimensions
WorkedExamples.Question: Your class creates a rectangular activity court scale diagram 14 cm long and 7 cm wide using 1 cm for 2 m. What are the full dimensions? If a 9 m bench segment must appear on the same scale, how long do you draw it?
WorkedExamples.Method: Label drawing measures and the units on a first-party geometric sketch; use a ruler to verify the produced representation.
Steps: Write the stated rate as 1 drawing cm to 2 actual m.
The 9 m bench should be 9÷2=4.5 cm long on the sketch.
Draw and label all segments and independently check the measured bench against the predicted length.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 28 m by 14 m court, 4.5 cm bench on the sketch.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher verifies measured diagram, scale key, labels and proportional geometry rather than the numbers alone.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using different units without conversion
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Ratio numbers cannot be compared before making dimensions consistent.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Convert units explicitly when simplifying the scale.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Dividing when finding actual length
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A 1 cm:2 m scale makes real distances larger.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check units and magnitude before choosing multiplication or division.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating a correctly computed numerical value as proof the complete drawing, construction, explanation or measured source task is satisfactory.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original activity includes creating or interpreting mathematical representations and defending the work to another person.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check every corresponding quantity, an accurate student sketch/measurement and written or oral justification with a teacher rubric; treat auto-marked arithmetic only as supporting practice.

SummaryPoints: Scales match drawing lengths with actual lengths.
Convert units before using a unitless ratio.
Use multiplication or division to move between drawing and reality.

Visuals.Title: Floor plan distance conversion
Visuals.Description: The model uses 1 cm on paper for 2 m of real distance. This first-party text table has labeled row headers so its numerical evidence is accessible without color or an image.

Lessons.Title: Scale Drawings and Maps
ExplanationParagraphs: Edulytiks learning target: Estimate route length from a map scale and relate it to constant speed and travel time. This is independently authored Grade 7 mathematics teaching aligned to the 2017–2019 OUR/IM source lesson. Source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/2/1/8/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0 source lineage; no publisher artwork reproduced).

Map routes can bend. Approximate them by several short segments, add scaled distances and then apply distance=speed×time. The source lesson is optional. The calculations and figures in the following examples were created for Edulytiks; they do not claim to reproduce the publisher's tasks or Cool Down.

Student task alignment: This lesson requires learners to compare road and direct distances on a scale map, with units and assumptions. Learner-produced figures, justification and peer discussion require teacher review; a numeric Practice score alone cannot certify that source goal.

KeyConcepts.Title: Curved-route estimate
KeyConcepts.Definition: A bent road can be approximated by straight map segments.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Add segment lengths before applying the scale.
KeyConcepts.Example: Segments 3 cm and 4 cm total 7 cm.

KeyConcepts.Title: Travel speed
KeyConcepts.Definition: Rate is distance traveled per unit time.
KeyConcepts.Rule: speed=distance÷time.
KeyConcepts.Example: 6 km in 3 h gives 2 km/h.

KeyConcepts.Title: Travel duration
KeyConcepts.Definition: Time equals distance divided by constant speed.
KeyConcepts.Rule: time=distance÷speed.
KeyConcepts.Example: 56 km at 28 km/h takes 2 h.

WorkedExamples.Title: Estimate a route
WorkedExamples.Question: A map uses 1 cm:1 km. Approximate a bend by segments 3 cm and 4 cm. How far is the route?
WorkedExamples.Check: The estimate improves if shorter segments follow the actual road.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find speed
WorkedExamples.Question: The estimated route distance is 6 km and the trip takes 3 h. Find average speed.
WorkedExamples.Check: 2 km/h for 3 h covers 6 km.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find time
WorkedExamples.Question: A road route is 56 km and the vehicle maintains 28 km/h. Find elapsed time.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare map route distance with straight-line distance
WorkedExamples.Question: On an original scale map, 1 cm represents 4 km. The marked road has three 2 cm segments, while the direct straight segment between the same endpoints measures 5 cm. Estimate each distance and explain which path is longer.
WorkedExamples.Method: Add the entire routed length, convert each drawing length with units, and distinguish a path from direct displacement.
Steps: Road drawing length=2+2+2=6 cm, representing 6×4=24 km.
Direct drawing length=5 cm, representing 5×4=20 km.
Compare 24 km road path to 20 km direct segment, a 4 km difference.
Explain that these are original schematic measurements; an unlabeled or not-to-scale map cannot support the same calculation.
WorkedExamples.Answer: The mapped road is about 24 km; the direct segment about 20 km; road path about 4 km longer.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher reviews route markings and the reason that a direct segment is not the traveled route.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using the straight-line distance as the full curved road
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A winding route is longer than its straight-line displacement.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Approximate along the route with several segments.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Mixing km with miles per hour
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Incompatible distance and speed units produce invalid time.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Convert distance and speed to compatible units first.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating a correctly computed numerical value as proof the complete drawing, construction, explanation or measured source task is satisfactory.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original activity includes creating or interpreting mathematical representations and defending the work to another person.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check every corresponding quantity, an accurate student sketch/measurement and written or oral justification with a teacher rubric; treat auto-marked arithmetic only as supporting practice.

SummaryPoints: Estimate bent routes by combining short distances.
Convert map lengths to actual distances.
Use distance, speed and time with consistent units.

Visuals.Title: Measuring a bent map route
Visuals.Description: Add consecutive segments along the route before converting using 1 cm for 1 km. This first-party text table has labeled row headers so its numerical evidence is accessible without color or an image.

Lessons.Title: Creating Scale Drawings
ExplanationParagraphs: Edulytiks learning target: Use actual measurements and a chosen scale to create a drawing; compare the drawing sizes produced by different scales. This is independently authored Grade 7 mathematics teaching aligned to the 2017–2019 OUR/IM source lesson. Source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/2/1/9/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0 source lineage; no publisher artwork reproduced).

A smaller real-world distance represented by each centimeter produces a larger drawing for the same object. Select scales that fit the available paper. The calculations and figures in the following examples were created for Edulytiks; they do not claim to reproduce the publisher's tasks or Cool Down.

Student task alignment: This lesson requires learners to measure and construct a floor plan with a complete scale key and peer review. Learner-produced figures, justification and peer discussion require teacher review; a numeric Practice score alone cannot certify that source goal.

KeyConcepts.Title: Creating a drawing
KeyConcepts.Definition: Find drawn length from measured length and scale.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Divide actual length by real-world units per drawing unit.
KeyConcepts.Example: 8 m on a 1 cm:2 m plan becomes 4 cm.

KeyConcepts.Title: Choosing a scale
KeyConcepts.Definition: A scale must fit the largest actual measurement on the page.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check both height and width before drawing.
KeyConcepts.Example: 8 m fits as 8 cm at 1 cm:1 m.

KeyConcepts.Title: Comparing two scales
KeyConcepts.Definition: The same object can have drawings of different sizes.
KeyConcepts.Rule: A scale representing more actual distance per cm produces smaller drawings.
KeyConcepts.Example: 1 cm:5 m produces a smaller drawing than 1 cm:2 m.

WorkedExamples.Title: Make a floor-plan rectangle
WorkedExamples.Question: A room measures 8 m by 5 m. Draw it using 1 cm:2 m.
WorkedExamples.Check: Every 1 cm represents 2 m.

WorkedExamples.Title: Choose the larger drawing
WorkedExamples.Question: The same 8 m wall is drawn at 1 cm:2 m and at 1 cm:1 m. Which is larger?
WorkedExamples.Answer: The 1 cm:1 m drawing is twice as long.
WorkedExamples.Check: A smaller real-length-per-centimeter scale makes a larger drawing.

WorkedExamples.Title: Convert a long wall
WorkedExamples.Question: An actual 15 m side is drawn with 1 cm:3 m. Find the drawing length.
WorkedExamples.Method: Divide by real distance per cm.
WorkedExamples.Check: The units are consistent.

WorkedExamples.Title: Produce a complete scale floor plan from field measurements
WorkedExamples.Question: Design a rectangular 7 m by 5 m studio with a 1.5 m-wide doorway along the 7 m wall. Choose 1 cm to 1 m, label the door and walls, and exchange the plan with another learner for error checks.
WorkedExamples.Method: Measure actual features, compute scale conversions, construct and label the plan, then revise based on feedback.
Steps: Create an initial sketch and record length 7 m, width 5 m and door width 1.5 m.
Under 1 cm:1 m, draw a 7-by-5 cm rectangle with a labeled 1.5 cm door opening.
Add a scale key and actual-length annotations for all critical segments.
Exchange the floor plan and check whether its labels, placement and doorway width can be reconstructed without verbal explanation.
WorkedExamples.Answer: An appropriately labeled 7-by-5 cm diagram with 1.5 cm door segment and scale 1 cm:1 m.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher-assessed drawing rubric: dimension accuracy, opening location, scale key, labels, completeness and peer revision.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Multiplying when constructing the drawing
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Applying real-world scale as a multiplier makes a huge drawing.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Divide measured real distance by the real distance represented per drawing unit.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Choosing a scale without checking page dimensions
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: One side may extend beyond the paper.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Test both planned dimensions before drawing.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating a correctly computed numerical value as proof the complete drawing, construction, explanation or measured source task is satisfactory.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original activity includes creating or interpreting mathematical representations and defending the work to another person.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check every corresponding quantity, an accurate student sketch/measurement and written or oral justification with a teacher rubric; treat auto-marked arithmetic only as supporting practice.

SummaryPoints: Convert each real measurement using the same scale.
Different scales can represent the same real object.
A usable scale fits the drawing medium.

Visuals.Title: Room scale drawing
Visuals.Description: Using 1 cm for 2 m, both floor-plan dimensions shrink by the same rule. This first-party text table has labeled row headers so its numerical evidence is accessible without color or an image.

Lessons.Title: Changing Scales in Scale Drawings
ExplanationParagraphs: Edulytiks learning target: Recreate a drawing at a new scale, compare areas and explain both ways to compute the new dimensions. This is independently authored Grade 7 mathematics teaching aligned to the 2017–2019 OUR/IM source lesson. Source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/2/1/10/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0 source lineage; no publisher artwork reproduced).

You may return to actual measurements first or directly compare two scale ratios. Either route must give identical new lengths. The calculations and figures in the following examples were created for Edulytiks; they do not claim to reproduce the publisher's tasks or Cool Down.

Student task alignment: This lesson requires learners to convert one original scale drawing to a new scale and explain the changed area. Learner-produced figures, justification and peer discussion require teacher review; a numeric Practice score alone cannot certify that source goal.

KeyConcepts.Title: Scale conversion via reality
KeyConcepts.Definition: Find actual length using the old scale, then drawn length using the new.
KeyConcepts.Rule: New drawing length=old drawing length×old real-units-per-cm/new real-units-per-cm.
KeyConcepts.Example: 3 cm at 4 m/cm becomes 6 cm at 2 m/cm.

KeyConcepts.Title: Direct drawing factor
KeyConcepts.Definition: The new-to-old drawing factor equals old denominator divided by new denominator.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Apply one factor to all drawn lengths.
KeyConcepts.Example: Changing 4 m/cm to 2 m/cm doubles drawn lengths.

KeyConcepts.Title: Area change
KeyConcepts.Definition: Area of the new drawn shape changes by the square of the drawing-length factor.
KeyConcepts.Rule: New drawing area=k²×old drawing area.
KeyConcepts.Example: Doubling drawing lengths quadruples its drawn area.

WorkedExamples.Title: Convert wall length
WorkedExamples.Question: An old plan uses 1 cm:4 m and shows a 3 cm wall. A new plan uses 1 cm:2 m.
WorkedExamples.Check: Both plans represent 12 m.

WorkedExamples.Title: Convert directly
WorkedExamples.Question: A 5 cm line is drawn at 1 cm:5 m. At 1 cm:10 m, how long should it be?
WorkedExamples.Check: New scale is half the drawing size.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare plan areas
WorkedExamples.Question: A rectangle measures 2 cm by 3 cm in the old plan. The new plan doubles its lengths. What area does the new drawing have?
WorkedExamples.Check: 4×old area=24; k²=4.

WorkedExamples.Title: Redraw the same plot using a second scale and compare areas
WorkedExamples.Question: A rectangular garden is drawn 10 cm by 6 cm at 1 cm:30 m. Make a new plan at 1 cm:20 m. Explain how the plans differ in size and squared area, then draw both.
WorkedExamples.Method: Recover actual dimensions, convert to a new rate, and calculate both drawing areas.
Steps: Actual lengths are 300 m and 180 m.
At 1 cm:20 m, the new diagram measures 15 cm by 9 cm.
Old drawing area=10×6=60 cm²; new drawing area=15×9=135 cm².
The linear ratio is 15/10=1.5; squared area ratio is 135/60=2.25.
WorkedExamples.Answer: New plan 15 by 9 cm, 2.25 times the old drawing area.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher checks both labeled original scale drawings and correctly distinguishes map area from actual land area.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Applying the old real units as the new drawing multiplier
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Scales must be compared in the correct direction.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Convert through actual measurements or use old/new scale ratio.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Scaling drawing area by the linear factor
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A two-dimensional area has two scaled dimensions.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use the square of the drawing factor.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating a correctly computed numerical value as proof the complete drawing, construction, explanation or measured source task is satisfactory.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original activity includes creating or interpreting mathematical representations and defending the work to another person.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check every corresponding quantity, an accurate student sketch/measurement and written or oral justification with a teacher rubric; treat auto-marked arithmetic only as supporting practice.

SummaryPoints: Change scales through real-world distances or a ratio of scale denominators.
Every drawing dimension changes by one common factor.
Drawing area changes by the square of that factor.

Visuals.Title: Changing plan scales
Visuals.Description: One wall drawn at 1 cm:4 m and 1 cm:2 m changes drawing length but not actual distance. This first-party text table has labeled row headers so its numerical evidence is accessible without color or an image.

Lessons.Title: Scales without Units
ExplanationParagraphs: Edulytiks learning target: Interpret and compare unitless scales such as 1:60; convert drawing and real measurements without confusing scale direction. This is independently authored Grade 7 mathematics teaching aligned to the 2017–2019 OUR/IM source lesson. Source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/2/1/11/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0 source lineage; no publisher artwork reproduced).

A 1:60 scale has no named units because both sides use the same length unit. Actual lengths are 60 times the drawing lengths. The calculations and figures in the following examples were created for Edulytiks; they do not claim to reproduce the publisher's tasks or Cool Down.

Student task alignment: This lesson requires learners to compare unitless and unit-bearing scales after converting units. Learner-produced figures, justification and peer discussion require teacher review; a numeric Practice score alone cannot certify that source goal.

KeyConcepts.Title: Unitless scale
KeyConcepts.Definition: A ratio a:b compares drawing and actual measurements in the same units.
KeyConcepts.Rule: For 1:60, multiply drawing lengths by 60.
KeyConcepts.Example: 3 cm on paper represents 180 cm in reality.

KeyConcepts.Title: Reverse ratio
KeyConcepts.Definition: Going from actual to drawing reverses the factor.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Multiply actual measurements by 1/60.
KeyConcepts.Example: 180 cm actual corresponds to 3 cm on paper.

KeyConcepts.Title: Comparing ratios
KeyConcepts.Definition: A 1:25 drawing is larger than a 1:100 drawing of the same item.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Smaller denominator means larger drawing at fixed actual size.
KeyConcepts.Example: A 100 cm edge draws 4 cm at 1:25, 1 cm at 1:100.

WorkedExamples.Title: Scale in centimeters
WorkedExamples.Question: A line measures 3 cm on a 1:60 scale drawing. Find its actual length.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use one ratio in matching units.
Steps: Convert 180 cm to 1.8 m if desired.
WorkedExamples.Check: The ratio is 1:60.

WorkedExamples.Title: Reverse the scale
WorkedExamples.Question: A real edge is 240 mm long and the drawing uses 1:60. Find its drawn length.
WorkedExamples.Check: The reverse scale is 1/60.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare scales
WorkedExamples.Question: An actual 100 cm edge is shown at 1:25 and 1:100. Which drawing is longer?
WorkedExamples.Answer: 1:25 gives a drawing four times as long.
WorkedExamples.Check: For the same actual length, the denominator and drawn size vary inversely.

WorkedExamples.Title: Explain whether two scale notations are equivalent
WorkedExamples.Question: One park map states 1 inch to 15 feet. Another states 1:180. Are these identical scales? Make a 6-foot wall segment at either scale and label the diagram.
WorkedExamples.Method: Convert feet to inches before writing a unitless scale; compare consistent lengths.
Steps: The first map has 1 drawing inch to 180 actual inches, or 1:180.
For a 6-foot wall: 72 actual inches divided by 180 gives 0.4 drawing inch.
Draw and label 0.4 inch with a scale key; report the conversion and units.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Yes; both scales are 1:180. A 6-foot wall is drawn 0.4 inch long.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher verifies the ruler diagram and requires same units before comparing unitless scale factors.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Applying 1:60 with different measurement units
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A unitless ratio assumes the units are the same on both sides.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Convert to the same unit before multiplying or dividing.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Reversing which side is drawing
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Using 60:1 instead of 1:60 swaps shrinking with enlarging.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Label which side belongs to the drawing and which to reality.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating a correctly computed numerical value as proof the complete drawing, construction, explanation or measured source task is satisfactory.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original activity includes creating or interpreting mathematical representations and defending the work to another person.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check every corresponding quantity, an accurate student sketch/measurement and written or oral justification with a teacher rubric; treat auto-marked arithmetic only as supporting practice.

SummaryPoints: Unitless scale compares like units.
At 1:n, actual length=n×drawing length.
A smaller n gives a larger drawing for the same real object.

Visuals.Title: Unitless 1:60 scale
Visuals.Description: Drawing and actual lengths are both in centimeters. This first-party text table has labeled row headers so its numerical evidence is accessible without color or an image.

Lessons.Title: Units in Scale Drawings
ExplanationParagraphs: Edulytiks learning target: Convert length units, recognize equivalent scale expressions and calculate real areas using a squared scale factor. This is independently authored Grade 7 mathematics teaching aligned to the 2017–2019 OUR/IM source lesson. Source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/2/1/12/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0 source lineage; no publisher artwork reproduced).

Two scales can sound different yet describe exactly the same geometric relationship. First put paired lengths in consistent units; for areas square the resulting linear factor. The calculations and figures in the following examples were created for Edulytiks; they do not claim to reproduce the publisher's tasks or Cool Down.

Student task alignment: This lesson requires learners to convert equivalent scales across units and explain squared area conversions. Learner-produced figures, justification and peer discussion require teacher review; a numeric Practice score alone cannot certify that source goal.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equivalent scales
KeyConcepts.Definition: Different unit expressions may yield the same unitless ratio.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Convert both scale lengths to the same unit.
KeyConcepts.Example: 1 inch:2.5 feet and 5 m:150 m are both 1:30.

KeyConcepts.Title: Unit conversion
KeyConcepts.Definition: Converting feet to inches multiplies by 12.
KeyConcepts.Rule: 1 ft=12 in and 1 m=100 cm.

KeyConcepts.Title: Area under map scale
KeyConcepts.Definition: Real area scales by the square of the real/drawing length factor.
KeyConcepts.Rule: At 1:30, area factor=900.
KeyConcepts.Example: 2 cm² on a plan corresponds to 1800 cm² in reality.

WorkedExamples.Title: Simplify customary units
WorkedExamples.Question: Express 1 inch to 2.5 feet as a unitless scale.
WorkedExamples.Check: Both sides were measured in inches.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare a metric scale
WorkedExamples.Question: Is 5 m:150 m equivalent to 1 in:2.5 ft?
WorkedExamples.Check: No physical units remain in the ratios.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find a real area
WorkedExamples.Question: An irregular polygon on a 1:30 plan has a computed drawing area of 2 cm². Find the actual area.

WorkedExamples.Title: Reconcile three unit-equivalent scales and compare areas
WorkedExamples.Question: A flag has actual dimensions 20 m by 12 m. At a unitless 1:100 scale, calculate its drawing dimensions in centimeters, then the actual and drawing areas. Explain why the areas have different unit scales.
WorkedExamples.Method: Convert all lengths to centimeters for the unitless ratio, then square the linear reduction.
Steps: Divide by 100 to get 20 cm by 12 cm in the drawing.
Actual area=240 m², or 2,400,000 cm²; drawing area=240 cm².
WorkedExamples.Answer: 20 cm by 12 cm drawing, 240 cm² drawing area, 240 m² actual area; unitless area factor is 10,000.
WorkedExamples.Check: A reader must not compare the bare numbers 240 m² and 240 cm² without unit conversion; label every measure.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Comparing inches directly with feet
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Raw 1:2.5 is not the same as 1 inch:2.5 feet.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Convert both parts to matching length units first.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Multiplying area by 30 rather than 900
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Area is a two-dimensional quantity.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Square the scale factor for area.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating a correctly computed numerical value as proof the complete drawing, construction, explanation or measured source task is satisfactory.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original activity includes creating or interpreting mathematical representations and defending the work to another person.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check every corresponding quantity, an accurate student sketch/measurement and written or oral justification with a teacher rubric; treat auto-marked arithmetic only as supporting practice.

SummaryPoints: Convert measurement units before simplifying scale ratios.
Equivalent scales have the same unitless ratio.
Real areas use the square of the real-to-drawing length factor.

Visuals.Title: Convert inch–foot scale units
Visuals.Description: The same ratio 1 inch to 2.5 feet becomes 1 inch to 30 inches. This first-party text table has labeled row headers so its numerical evidence is accessible without color or an image.

Lessons.Title: Draw It to Scale
ExplanationParagraphs: Edulytiks learning target: Plan, measure, construct and justify a scale floor plan with checked dimensions and a human-reviewed explanation. This is independently authored Grade 7 mathematics teaching aligned to the 2017–2019 OUR/IM source lesson. Source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/2/1/13/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0 source lineage; no publisher artwork reproduced).

This optional project combines classroom measurements, suitable paper choice, spatial layout and reasoned scale selection. Original floor plans and oral critique require teacher review, not a single auto-graded response. The calculations and figures in the following examples were created for Edulytiks; they do not claim to reproduce the publisher's tasks or Cool Down.

Student task alignment: This lesson requires learners to produce, present, revise and justify an authentic measured floor plan. Learner-produced figures, justification and peer discussion require teacher review; a numeric Practice score alone cannot certify that source goal.

KeyConcepts.Title: Measurement plan
KeyConcepts.Definition: A floor plan begins with selected real distances and accurate units.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Measure the main walls, door placements and fixed obstacles.
KeyConcepts.Example: Record room width 6 m and length 8 m.

KeyConcepts.Title: Fit to paper
KeyConcepts.Definition: Choose a scale that makes all features fit the page.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check longest drawn dimension against page size.
KeyConcepts.Example: At 1 cm:1 m, an 8 m wall is drawn 8 cm.

KeyConcepts.Title: Teacher-reviewed justification
KeyConcepts.Definition: A correct plan explains measurement decisions, scale, labels and spatial fidelity.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use a rubric for accuracy, layout, units and explanation.
KeyConcepts.Example: Two students may choose different valid scales.

WorkedExamples.Title: Create a rectangular room plan
WorkedExamples.Question: A room measures 8 m by 6 m. Use scale 1 cm:1 m. What rectangle should you draw?
Steps: Label the dimensions and scale on the plan.
WorkedExamples.Check: Both dimensions preserve 1 cm per real metre.

WorkedExamples.Title: Check page constraints
WorkedExamples.Question: Your page has a 20 cm by 15 cm available space. A 10 m by 8 m room uses 1 cm:0.5 m. Will it fit?
WorkedExamples.Answer: No; the 16 cm side exceeds 15 cm.
WorkedExamples.Check: Use a smaller drawing scale, such as 1 cm:1 m, to fit.

WorkedExamples.Title: Review a scale proposal
WorkedExamples.Question: Two students draw the same 8 m wall at 1 cm:2 m and 1 cm:1 m. May both plans be valid?
WorkedExamples.Method: Assess scale consistency rather than identical drawing size.
Steps: Check that each student's other dimensions use their chosen scale too.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Both plans can be correct if each is consistently scaled and labeled.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher reviews measurements, relative placements and an explanation of scale choice.

WorkedExamples.Title: Teacher-reviewed classroom floor plan and peer critique
WorkedExamples.Question: Using original measurements (room 8 m long and 6 m wide, doorway 1 m, board 3 m), design a floor plan at an appropriate scale for A4 paper. Include measured openings, a legend, actual units, and a peer-revision note.
WorkedExamples.Method: Plan, estimate, measure, choose a feasible consistent scale, construct, exchange, critique and revise; no single numeric answer certifies this project.
Steps: Choose 1 cm:1 m to make a 8-by-6 cm room drawing that fits ordinary A4 paper.
Mark the 1 cm doorway opening and a 3 cm board in physically plausible locations.
Label actual room dimensions, openings and the scale; organize feature measurements for another reader.
Exchange plans, identify at least one placement, completeness or scale issue, and revise before submitting the final diagram.
WorkedExamples.Answer: A student-created, feasible, fully labeled scale drawing and a revision explanation; multiple correct designs exist.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher-only rubric: measured geometry, scale, consistent units, correct features, clarity, partner feedback and revision.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating the classroom task as an exact-number quiz
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: An authentic plan requires drawing, measurement, communication and critique.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Teacher reviews a drawing against a rubric, including accuracy and clarity.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Changing the scale between objects
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: This produces inconsistent placement and relative dimensions.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Apply the chosen scale to every room feature and label it.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating a correctly computed numerical value as proof the complete drawing, construction, explanation or measured source task is satisfactory.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original activity includes creating or interpreting mathematical representations and defending the work to another person.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check every corresponding quantity, an accurate student sketch/measurement and written or oral justification with a teacher rubric; treat auto-marked arithmetic only as supporting practice.

SummaryPoints: Measure and sketch real dimensions before drawing.
Choose one scale that fits the paper and use it consistently.
Have a teacher review the drawing, measurement decisions and explanation.
